This is meant to be a thread about what small changes, collectively, can lead to weight loss. I'll start with some personal background and then a specific question, and I would love to hear your own anecdotes about small habit changes that had positive effects for you.

I'm 40, 5'11 and 210lbs. My high school weight was 172 and until my mid-30's I maintained at about 185. I was stocky, and did some fighting, so I was in decent shape and strong but never "ripped".

Through my 20's I developed PTSD which somehow manifested in more extreme ways when I was removed from the situations that caused it. [Idle hands?] In my mid 30's I experienced a great personal loss and since then my weight just started climbing to where I am today.

About 5 months ago I was at my all-time peak of 220 and decided that I had to change. But all of the things that used to work for me to shed a few extra pounds didn't seem to make a dent.

Recently I quit drinking diet soda or anything with artificial sweeteners due to the numerous scientific studies which show they actually aggravate weight gain. I had fooled myself that this was only applicable to Aspartame but recently have read more studies which include other artificial sweeteners I thought were "safe".

So a few weeks later I have already lost 5 lbs after losing the first 5 through simple mindfulness and better diet choices. I also bought some weights just to do some low-rep strength exercises daily which I will pyramid over time. I made the conscious decision to try and control my gut bacteria - so I am now supplementing with 2 different types of probiotics. [Several of the studies point to artificial sweeteners, again, as helping cultivate types of gut bacteria associated with obesity]

I am not going to lie, I still have bad habits. My diet has improved but there are still more carbs than I know I should eat. My willpower and mood seem to have improved noticeably since I cut out diet sodas, and it is easier to make the right decisions. But I still drink about 40 oz of beer a few times a week. It helps me sleep but it isn't even enough to get me drunk. In my 20's I didn't drink beer, and I'm sure this is part of my problem.

So here is my question:

I just bought a bike and have committed myself to riding 3 miles a day. I figure it is getting my heart-rate up for at least 15-30 minutes each day which is mainly the reason I bought it.

What are your predictions as to whether this will actually make a difference? I will be doing around 15 miles 5-days a week beginning January due to a new personal situation. I installed a weight-tracking app on my phone and will be happy to revisit this thread later with updates.
